status.en: 7 armed incidents reported in the past seven days, 67% fewer than the week before, most of them in La Espriella, Planadas and Bogota.
status.nb: 7 væpnede hendelser meldt de siste sju dagene, 67 prosent færre enn uken før, flest i La Espriella, Planadas og Bogota.

summary.en: The Colombian government has engaged U.S. intelligence and struck a deal with Venezuela to secure the release of two ELN hostages while President De la Espriella faces a surge of violence, including the killing of over 45 social leaders in his first 100 days. Petro has been accused of freezing the purchase of equipment to counter armed-group drones, and U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth arrived in Bogotá to reinforce the security agenda. In Kyiv, a 19‑year-old woman was detained for poisoning a Colombian veteran of the Ukrainian Armed Forces for $1,000. Colombian land defenders continue to face lawfare and smear campaigns linked to a Canadian-owned copper project. The conflict recorded 225 battle-related deaths in 2024, according to UCDP.
summary.nb: Den colombianske regjeringen har involvert amerikansk etterretning og inngått en avtale med Venezuela for å sikre løslatelsen av to ELN-gisler, mens president De la Espriella står overfor en voldsbølge, inkludert drapet på over 45 samfunnsledere i sine første 100 dager. Petro er blitt anklaget for å ha fryst kjøpet av utstyr for å motvirke droner fra væpnede grupper, og USAs forsvarsminister Pete Hegseth ankom Bogotá for å styrke sikkerhetsagendaen. I Kyiv ble en 19‑år gammel kvinne pågrepet for å ha forgiftet en colombiansk veteran fra den ukrainske væpnede styrken for 1 000 dollar. Colombianske landforsvarere fortsetter å møte lovkrig og sm smear-kampanjer knyttet til et kanadisk-eid kobberprosjekt. Konflikten registrerte 225 dødsfall knyttet til kamper i 2024, ifølge UCDP.

background.title: Colombian conflict
background.extract: The Colombian conflict began on May 27, 1964, and is a low-intensity asymmetric war between the government of Colombia, paramilitary groups, crime syndicates, and far-left guerrilla groups engaged in armed factional hostilities to increase their influence in Colombian territory. Some of the most important international contributors to the Colombian conflict include multinational corporations, the United States, Cuba, and the drug trafficking industry.
